stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?
stimulus: A marine biologist marks two survey lines across a reef, $\ell$ and $m$, with $\ell$ lying above $m$ on her chart. A guide rope, $t$, crosses $\ell$ at point $P$ and $m$ at point $Q$. At $P$, the angle above $\ell$ and to the right of $t$ measures $112^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
choices: The angle at $P$ below $\ell$ and left of $t$ measures $112^\circ$.
The angle at $Q$ above $m$ and left of $t$ measures $68^\circ$.
The angle at $P$ above $\ell$ and left of $t$ measures $68^\circ$.
The angle at $Q$ below $m$ and right of $t$ measures $112^\circ$.
explanation: The angle at $P$ below $\ell$ and right of $t$ forms a linear pair with the $112^\circ$ angle, so it measures $68^\circ$. It lies between the lines on the right of $t$. The angle at $Q$ above $m$ and left of $t$ lies between the lines on the left of $t$, so the two are alternate interior angles. If both measure $68^\circ$, the alternate interior angles are equal, and that proves $\ell \parallel m$.

A.why: This angle is vertical to the $112^\circ$ angle, so it is $112^\circ$ whether or not the lines are parallel. You picked a fact that is always true where two lines cross. It says nothing about line $m$.

C.why: This angle forms a linear pair with the $112^\circ$ angle, so it is always $68^\circ$. It involves only line $\ell$ and gives no link to $m$. You fell for the straight-line fact that holds every time.

D.why: This angle and the given angle are on the same side of $t$ and both outside the lines, so for parallel lines they would sum to $180^\circ$. Here $112 + 112 = 224$, which actually shows the lines are not parallel. You treated a same-side pair as if it were alternate.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$?
stimulus: A textile historian is comparing triangular gussets cut for two antique smocks. In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 6$ centimeters and $BC = 9$ centimeters. In triangle $DEF$, $DE = 4$ centimeters and $EF = 6$ centimeters.
explanation: $\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}$ and $\frac{BC}{EF} = \frac{9}{6} = \frac{3}{2}$, so two pairs of sides are in proportion. Angle $B$ lies between $AB$ and $BC$, and angle $E$ lies between $DE$ and $EF$. If those included angles are congruent, SAS similarity proves the triangles similar.

A.why: Angle $C$ is not between the two proportional sides; it is opposite $AB$. Proportional sides plus a non-included angle is SSA. A non-similar triangle can fit the same conditions, so this does not prove similarity.

B.why: Angle $E$ corresponds to angle $B$, not angle $A$. Matching angles at non-corresponding vertices does not complete any similarity criterion. Identify which angle sits between the proportional sides before you match letters.

D.why: $\frac{AC}{DF} = \frac{6}{9} = \frac{2}{3}$, but the other ratios are $\frac{3}{2}$. You saw the numbers 6 and 9 and assumed the ratio matched without checking which side goes on top. The three ratios are not equal, so SSS similarity fails.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $PQR$ is congruent to triangle $STU$?
stimulus: A folklore scholar draws two triangular charts to compare how often motifs appear in two versions of a legend. In triangle $PQR$, angle $Q$ is a right angle. In triangle $STU$, angle $T$ is a right angle.
explanation: Both triangles are right triangles. $PR$ and $SU$ are the hypotenuses, since each is opposite the right angle. $QR$ and $TU$ are corresponding legs. A congruent hypotenuse and a congruent leg prove the triangles congruent by HL.

A.why: Matching all three angles shows the triangles have the same shape, not the same size. Angles alone (AAA) prove similarity, never congruence. You need at least one pair of equal sides.

C.why: $QR$ is a leg of triangle $PQR$, but $SU$ is the hypotenuse of triangle $STU$. Setting a leg equal to a hypotenuse does not match corresponding parts, and then $PR$ is longer than $SU$, so the triangles can't be congruent.

D.why: Angle $T$ was already given as a right angle, so the only new fact here is the hypotenuse. A right angle and a hypotenuse without a matching leg are not enough. Many different right triangles share the same hypotenuse.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?
stimulus: On an agricultural test plot, two irrigation channels run along lines $\ell$ and $m$, with $\ell$ above $m$ on the site map. A drainage cut along line $t$ crosses $\ell$ at point $P$ and $m$ at point $Q$. Angle 1 is at $P$, above $\ell$ and to the right of $t$, and measures $(2x + 14)^\circ$. Angle 2 is at $Q$, above $m$ and to the left of $t$, and measures $(4x - 8)^\circ$. Angle 4 is at $P$, below $\ell$ and to the left of $t$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Angle 1 is vertical to angle 4, and angle 4 lies between the lines on the left of $t$, as angle 2 does. Angles 4 and 2 are same-side interior angles, so the lines are parallel exactly when $m\angle 1 + m\angle 2 = 180$. That gives $(2x + 14) + (4x - 8) = 180$, so $6x + 6 = 180$ and $x = 29$. Then the angles measure $72^\circ$ and $108^\circ$, which sum to $180^\circ$.

A.why: You set the two angles equal: $2x + 14 = 4x - 8$. That is the test for corresponding or alternate angles, but these angles are a same-side pair, which must be supplementary. At $x = 11$ both are $36^\circ$, so the lines are not parallel.

C.why: Angle 4 is vertical to angle 1, so it equals $(2x + 14)^\circ$ whenever $t$ crosses $\ell$. A fact that is always true can't prove anything about parallel lines.

D.why: You dropped the constants and solved $6x = 180$. The equation is $6x + 6 = 180$. At $x = 30$ the angles sum to $186^\circ$, not $180^\circ$.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ADE$ is similar to triangle $ABC$?
stimulus: An astronomer models the sightlines from a telescope at point $A$ to two stars at points $B$ and $C$ as triangle $ABC$, where $AB = 12$, $AC = 18$, and $BC = 10$, in arbitrary units. Point $D$ lies on $\overline{AB}$ and point $E$ lies on $\overline{AC}$, forming a smaller triangle $ADE$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: The two triangles share angle $A$. $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{9}{18} = \frac{1}{2}$, so the sides on either side of angle $A$ are in proportion. Because angle $A$ is the included angle, SAS similarity proves the triangles similar.

A.why: Both ratios equal $\frac{1}{2}$, but angle $A$ is not between $AD$ and $DE$; it is opposite $DE$. This is SSA. Since $DE$ is shorter than $AD$, a second, non-similar triangle also fits, so it proves nothing.

B.why: Cutting the same length off each side is subtraction, not scaling. It gives $AD = 6$ and $AE = 12$, so the ratios are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{2}{3}$, which are not equal.

D.why: Both ratios are $\frac{1}{2}$, but angle $A$ is opposite $DE$, not between $AE$ and $DE$. Proportional sides with a non-included angle (SSA) do not fix the triangle's shape, so similarity is not proved.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?
stimulus: A musicologist sketches the frame of a harp as a triangle. Points $B$ and $C$ lie on line $m$, and point $A$ lies above $m$. Line $\ell$ passes through $A$, with point $D$ on $\ell$ to the left of $A$ and point $E$ on $\ell$ to the right of $A$, so that $D$ is on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ as $B$'s left and $E$ is on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{AC}$ as $C$'s right. In triangle $ABC$, $m\angle BAC = 40^\circ$ and $m\angle ACB = 65^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: From the triangle sum, $m\angle ABC = 180 - 40 - 65 = 75^\circ$. With $\overline{AB}$ as the transversal, $\angle DAB$ and $\angle ABC$ are alternate interior angles. If $m\angle DAB = 75^\circ$, those alternate interior angles are equal, which proves $\ell \parallel m$.

B.why: $65^\circ$ is angle $ACB$, which pairs with $\angle EAC$ across transversal $\overline{AC}$, not with $\angle DAB$. You matched $\angle DAB$ to the wrong angle of the triangle.

C.why: $105^\circ$ is $40 + 65$, the exterior angle at $B$. That is a step toward the answer, not the answer. Angle $DAB$ must equal the interior angle $ABC$, which is $75^\circ$, so $105^\circ$ would mean the lines are not parallel.

D.why: $\angle DAB$ and $\angle BAE$ form a linear pair on $\ell$, so they always sum to $180^\circ$. That is true however $\ell$ is tilted, so it proves nothing about parallel lines.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $JKL$ is similar to triangle $MNP$?
stimulus:
A linguist uses triangles $JKL$ and $MNP$ to represent the vowel spaces of two related dialects. It is known that $\angle J \cong \angle M$. Each statement below is to be considered separately, on its own, alongside this given fact.

I. $\angle K \cong \angle N$
II. $\frac{JK}{MN} = \frac{JL}{MP}$
III. $\frac{JK}{MN} = \frac{KL}{NP}$
explanation: Statement I gives a second pair of congruent angles, so the triangles are similar by AA. Statement II makes the sides on either side of angle $J$ proportional to the sides on either side of angle $M$, and the congruent angle lies between them, so the triangles are similar by SAS. Statement III pairs $JK$ with $KL$, but angle $J$ is opposite $KL$ rather than between the two sides. That is SSA, which does not prove similarity.

A.why: You saw that I works by AA but missed that II also works on its own. The given angle $J$ lies between $JK$ and $JL$, so proportional sides around it complete SAS similarity.

C.why: You ruled out I, probably because angles alone are never enough for congruence. Similarity is different: two pairs of congruent angles prove it by AA. You also accepted III, which is SSA.

D.why: Statement III gives proportional sides, but angle $J$ is not between $JK$ and $KL$. Proportional sides with a non-included angle (SSA) do not prove similarity, so III should be excluded.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $AEB$ is congruent to triangle $CED$?
stimulus: An immunologist sketches the crossing arms of two antibody fragments as segments $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$, which intersect at point $E$. Triangles $AEB$ and $CED$ are formed on opposite sides of $E$. It is given that $AE = CE$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: You already have $AE = CE$, and $\angle AEB \cong \angle CED$ because they are vertical angles. Adding $BE = DE$ gives two pairs of congruent sides with the included angle between them. That proves the triangles congruent by SAS.

A.why: These are vertical angles, so they are congruent whenever two segments cross. You already had this for free, so it adds nothing. One side and one angle is not a congruence criterion.

C.why: With the vertical angles, this gives two sides and an angle, but the angle at $E$ is not between $AE$ and $AB$. That is SSA, which does not guarantee congruence.

D.why: Angle $ABE$ corresponds to angle $CDE$, not angle $DCE$. Matching angles at non-corresponding vertices does not complete ASA or AAS. Check which vertex matches which before you use an angle pair.
